segments.say: We often think of deep closeness as something that can only grow slowly, over many years. Old friends, long marriages, the people who've known us forever. And there's truth in that. Time matters. But researchers have found that the way people spend their time together may matter just as much. And one study suggested that the right kind of conversation can create a surprising sense of closeness in under an hour.

show.title: Myth eleven: closeness just takes years

segments.say: In 1997, Arthur Aron, Elaine Aron and their colleagues paired up students who were strangers. For about forty-five minutes, the pairs took turns asking each other a set of thirty-six questions, given to them in three sets. The questions started light and gradually became more personal.

show.what: The experimental generation of interpersonal closeness: a procedure and some preliminary findings

segments.say: Early questions were gentle, like, given the choice of anyone in the world, whom would you want as a dinner guest? Later ones went deeper, like, what is your most treasured memory? And near the end, people were asked to share a personal problem and ask for the other person's advice on how they might handle it.

show.title: How the questions build
items: Early: given the choice of anyone in the world, whom would you want as a dinner guest?
Middle: what do you value most in a friendship?
Later: what is your most treasured memory?
Last: share a personal problem and ask your partner's advice

segments.say: Other pairs spent the same amount of time making small talk, with questions like, what was the best gift you ever received and why? Afterwards, the pairs who had answered the gradually deepening questions felt noticeably closer to each other than those who had made small talk. The questions became famous years later, often called the thirty-six questions to fall in love.

It's worth saying clearly that the study was about closeness, not love. Most pairs didn't fall in love. But they did feel genuinely closer, more quickly than you might expect from a single conversation with a stranger. The key wasn't the specific questions. It was the gradual, mutual opening up.
That idea of mutual opening up has a long history in psychology, and a well-known review put numbers on it.

In 1994, Nancy Collins and Lynn Carol Miller combined many studies on self-disclosure, sharing personal information about ourselves. They found three linked patterns. People who disclose more tend to be liked more. People tend to disclose more to those they already like. And people tend to like others more after disclosing to them.

show.what: Self-disclosure and liking: a meta-analytic review

segments.say: So sharing and liking feed each other, in a gentle upward spiral. You share a little. The other person responds warmly and shares something back. You both feel a little closer, and so you share a little more. That's how many close relationships grow. Not in one leap, but in small steps, taken together.

Researchers like Harry Reis and Phillip Shaver have argued that the most important part of this process isn't the sharing itself. It's how the other person responds. When you share something and feel understood, valued and cared for, closeness grows. When you share and feel ignored or judged, it doesn't. Reis calls this perceived partner responsiveness.
And there's a simple way to show responsiveness that most of us don't use nearly enough. Asking questions.

In 2017, Karen Huang and her colleagues at Harvard studied conversations between strangers, including chats online and real speed dates. People who asked more questions, especially follow-up questions that built on what the other person had just said, were liked more by their conversation partners.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2017
show.what: It doesn't hurt to ask: question-asking increases liking

segments.say: Follow-up questions seem to be especially powerful because they show that you were really listening. Oh, you grew up by the sea, what was that like? It's a small thing. But it tells the other person that their words landed, and that you want to know more about them.
So deeper conversation brings people closer. Why don't we do it more often? A study published in 2022 offered an answer.

Michael Kardas, Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley asked strangers to have either shallow or deep conversations with each other. Before talking, people predicted how awkward the conversations would be and how much they'd enjoy them. Afterwards, they reported how it had actually gone.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2022
show.what: Overly shallow? Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation

segments.say: People consistently expected deep conversations to be more awkward and less enjoyable than they turned out to be. They also underestimated how interested their partners would be in hearing about their thoughts and feelings. In reality, the deep conversations left people feeling more connected, and they weren't nearly as uncomfortable as feared.

So one reason we stick to small talk is a simple misjudgement. We think others don't want to go deeper, and they think the same about us. Everyone stays politely on the surface, when many of us would actually welcome something more meaningful.
Still, depth isn't everything. Time does matter. And one researcher tried to work out roughly how much of it friendship takes.

In 2019, Jeffrey Hall at the University of Kansas surveyed adults who had recently moved to a new city, and students starting university. He asked them about the new people they had met, how much time they had spent together, and how close they had become.

show.where: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 2019
show.what: How many hours does it take to make a friend?

segments.say: His estimates suggested that it took roughly fifty hours together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, around ninety hours to become a friend, and more than two hundred hours to become a close friend. And it mattered how the time was spent. Time spent joking, catching up and talking about meaningful things helped more than time spent just working side by side.

So closeness takes both. Time, yes, often a lot of it. But also the right kind of time. Conversations that go a little deeper, questions that show we're listening, and the willingness to share something real and respond warmly when someone shares with us.

Gradually deepening conversation. Taking turns to open up. Responding with warmth. Asking follow-up questions. And spending real time together. None of these are secrets. But knowing that they work, and that most people would welcome them more than we expect, might give us a little courage to try.

And courage is exactly what the next chapter is about. Because there's a strange gap between how much we think people like us after a conversation, and how much they actually do. Most of us get it wrong, and in the same direction.
